requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) serves lan-a addresses to node3 from its own pool with itself as default gateway
requirements.summary: eth2 set to 10.50.10.254/24; Kea DHCPv4 configured with pool 10.50.10.100-.200, default-router 10.50.10.254, subnet-id 1, service confirmed active. node3's eth1 (via a new NetworkManager DHCP profile) obtained 10.50.10.100/24 with default route 10.50.10.254 and successfully pinged the gateway. Lease file on node1 shows node3's MAC bound to 10.50.10.100. Confirmed again after a full reboot of both node1 and node3, with node3 automatically reacquiring the same lease/route without executor intervention, demonstrating persistence.

requirements.requirement: node2 (OPNsense) serves lan-b addresses to node4 from its own pool with itself as default gateway
requirements.summary: opt2/vtnet2 set to 10.60.10.254/24; Kea DHCPv4 subnet 10.60.10.0/24 configured with pool 10.60.10.100-.200 and router option 10.60.10.254, generated into kea-dhcp4.conf and running. A pre-existing factory dnsmasq service squatting UDP/67 was diagnosed (DHCPSRV_OPEN_SOCKET_FAIL) and permanently disabled via config.xml + template reload so Kea could bind. node4's eth1 obtained 10.60.10.100/24 with default route 10.60.10.254 via DHCP and pinged the gateway. After a full reboot of node2 and node4, the fix was found not fully persistent on first pass (dnsmasq respawned), was re-applied via the canonical config.xml path, and node4 automatically reacquired its lease/route again, confirming the corrected persistent state.

requirements.requirement: node3 and node4 obtain addressing from the router in front of them rather than from static configuration
requirements.summary: node3 and node4 each had no prior static configuration on their lan-facing interface (eth1); the executor created persistent NetworkManager DHCP profiles (ipv4.method auto) on eth1 for each, which acquired addresses/routes from their respective routers and, critically, re-acquired the same addressing automatically after a full reboot with no executor re-configuration, confirming the DHCP client config (not static) is what drives addressing.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on all four managed nodes (independent of public task contract)
requirements.summary: All four nodes show a pre-restart boot identity/health capture, a restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/data/route state: node1 (Kea + lease + eth2 intact, node3 reachable), node2 (Kea clean after re-applying the persistent dnsmasq fix, lease intact, node4 reachable), node3 (auto DHCP reacquisition, route, ping), node4 (auto DHCP reacquisition, route, ping). This is cross-checked against the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot, which independently shows all four boot identities changed relative to before-prepare.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct, corroborating evidence: node1 (VyOS) and node2 (OPNsense) each serve DHCP on their own LAN segment to their directly connected RHEL client, handing out addresses from their own pool and themselves as default gateway, and node3/node4 now obtain addressing dynamically rather than statically. The executor additionally ran the full node-restart evidence protocol on all four nodes, capturing pre-restart boot identity/health, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/route state — including catching and correctly fixing a non-persistent dnsmasq workaround on node2 that resurfaced after reboot. Operational hygiene is generally good: exploratory topology-mapping mutations and a failed dnsmasq troubleshooting attempt were bounded and reverted/corrected, though small residual files (/tmp/reboot.log on node3/node4, /tmp/n3e1.log on node3) were left behind.
limitations: Package-manager health checks on node3 and node4 timed out in both the before-prepare and after-executor snapshots, so native package-state integrity could not be independently confirmed for the RHEL nodes.

The node2 dnsmasq fix required a second corrective pass after the first restart revealed it was not fully persistent; while the final state is confirmed clean, this indicates the original fix verification before restart was not fully reliable evidence of persistence on its own.
Minor unremoved temporary artifacts (/tmp/reboot.log on node3 and node4, /tmp/n3e1.log on node3) were not independently confirmed as harmless beyond their small size and content.

operational_hygiene.summary: Overall clean: temporary DHCP/broadcast probe IPs added to node3/node4 eth1 (169.254.9.1/.2) and node2 vtnet1/vtnet2 (169.254.9.3) during topology discovery were all removed within the same or a subsequent command (cmd-e24aa9c28e6246a1, cmd-8d3f493159fb45b2, inline deletes in cmd-77a6032df48e4702). On node2, an initial troubleshooting attempt directly edited /usr/local/etc/dnsmasq.conf (added bind-interfaces) and used `service dnsmasq restart`/`sysrc dnsmasq_enable=NO` outside the OPNsense config.xml-managed path (cmd-6b10e694560f446a, cmd-c1d73aa29c97430d); this did not resolve the issue and was reverted (dnsmasq.conf restored from backup, cmd-e484826d092341ca) in favor of the canonical config.xml + template-reload fix, which is an acceptable corrective sequence rather than an abandoned mutation. Scratch files used to manipulate config.xml on node2 (/tmp/f_*.py, kea_apply.php, dnsmasq_apply.php, fw_apply.php, rules.debug, dnsmasq.conf.bak) and node1's /tmp/reboot.log were explicitly cleaned up at the end (cmd-bfd71b76eb20496d, cmd-38011eec3bcc478e). However, /tmp/reboot.log was left behind on node3 and node4 (visible in the after-executor snapshot), and node3 also retained a stray /tmp/n3e1.log from a failed tcpdump probe attempt (cmd-6dc9dbd2afcc49b8, which failed with 'tcpdump: command not found' since node3 lacks tcpdump) — these are small, low-risk, non-security-relevant residue that were never cleaned up.
